blocks.text:
# Welcome
Welcome to your first lesson. Today is about getting your bearings: finding your way around the keys, learning how your fingers are numbered, and how to sit and hold your hands when you're at a real keyboard. You won't read any music yet, and you won't need any note names. Those come in the next lessons, once the keyboard feels familiar.

By the end of this lesson you'll be able to find any group of two or three black keys without hints, name your fingers 1 to 5, copy a short pattern you see and hear, and you'll have tried sitting and shaping your hand at a real keyboard (something to keep coming back to: the app can't see it). Two parts are scored by the app, finding the groups and the copying game; the rest you'll check for yourself at the end.

# The black keys are your map
Look at the black keys for a moment. They aren't spread evenly: they come in little groups, **two together**, then a gap, then **three together**, then a gap, all the way along the keyboard. That pattern is your map. Every key on the piano can be found from it, so before we name any keys, let's get to know the groups.

A **gap** is a place where two white keys sit side by side with no black key between them. Each group of black keys has a gap on either side.

Keys to the **left** sound **lower**; keys to the **right** sound **higher**.

blocks.alt: Two octaves of piano keys: groups of two black keys outlined in orange and labelled 2, groups of three outlined in blue and labelled 3, a gap between two white keys marked "no black key here", and arrows showing lower to the left and higher to the right
blocks.caption: Groups of two (orange) and three (blue), with a gap between them.

blocks.text:
# Your first sounds
Tap **Start** below to open the keys. On the screen the black keys are outlined in their groups, an orange line round each **two** and a blue one round each **three**. Tap the two black keys of a pair, one after the other. Then tap › to move higher up the piano and play a pair there, and ‹ to come back down, past where you started, and play a pair low down. The small drawing of the whole piano above the keys shows where you are. Then do the same with the groups of three.

Use whichever finger is comfortable on the screen. Hear how the sound climbs as you go right and falls as you go left. When you're done, come back here with ←.

blocks.title: Your first sounds
blocks.about: Pairs, then threes: here, higher up (›) and lower down (‹). Nothing is scored.

blocks.text:
# Find the groups
Now a check of what you've found. Each card names a group, "a group of three" or "a group of two, lower down": find it and tap any key of it. The screen shows only part of the piano, so use ‹ and › to move along it; the small drawing above the keys shows where you are. Each card starts somewhere new, so look for the pattern, not for a spot you remember. "Lower down" means the lowest one you can reach, "higher up" the highest. There's no clock, and if you tap the wrong place the app shows you the right group.

blocks.title: Find the groups
blocks.doneWhen: 5 of the 6 cards right first time
blocks.about: Find the group each card names and tap any key of it; ‹ › move along the piano.

blocks.text:
# At a real keyboard: sitting
The next few sections are about your body at a real piano or keyboard. The app can't check any of this, so try it whenever you're at a keyboard, or practise it at a table now. How you sit decides how freely your arms and hands can move, so it's worth setting up carefully once. The video after this section shows each point.

Sit **toward the front of the seat**, not right on the edge, facing the middle of the keys. That leaves you free to lean a little left or right as your hands travel up and down the keyboard, without twisting.

Sit **tall** and let your arms **hang loosely** from your shoulders. With your fingers on the keys, your **elbows** should sit a little in front of your body, not tucked against your sides, and your **forearm** should be about level from elbow to knuckles. If your forearm slopes up to the keys, the seat is too low; if it slopes down, too high. (An ordinary chair is often too low.)

To check the **distance**, stretch your arms straight out with loose fists: your knuckles should just touch the panel behind the keys (on a piano, the fallboard: the lid that folds down over them; on a portable keyboard, the edge of the case just behind the keys). Take this as a starting guide: then let your elbows bend and hang, and check that they sit a little in front of your body and that you can reach the keys comfortably.

Rest your **feet flat** on the floor.

blocks.title: What Is Proper Piano Posture? Tips for Hand, Arm, and Seat Position (Hoffman Academy, 14 min)
blocks.caption: Made for children; it covers where to sit, how far away and how high, and the shape of the hand.

blocks.text:
# At a real keyboard: a round hand
Pianists play with a **round hand**: fingers gently curved, so they land on their tips. A round hand is strong without being tight, and every finger can reach its key easily.

Here's a way to find the shape. Let your arms hang by your sides and relax your hands completely; they curve on their own. Now lift one hand onto the keys, or the table, without changing that shape. Your fingers make a letter **C**, with the fingertips resting on the surface and the thumb resting lightly beside them.

If your hand feels stiff, imagine you're holding an apple in each hand, then **drop the apples**: your wrists go soft and your fingers stay curved. That softness is what you want to keep.

# Your finger numbers
In piano music, fingers are named by numbers, the same way in both hands:

- **1**: thumb
- **2**: pointer
- **3**: middle finger
- **4**: ring finger
- **5**: little finger

So both thumbs are 1, and both little fingers are 5.

Try this on the table: rest both hands in a round shape and tap each finger as you say its number out loud, 1 to 5 and back. Then try them out of order, naming the hand first: right hand 3, left hand 1, right hand 5, left hand 2, right hand 4. Saying the number while you move the finger is what makes it stick.

blocks.title: Piano Finger Numbers for Beginners (Hoffman Academy, 7 min)
blocks.caption: Made for children: finger numbers with games.
Right hand: fingers 2 and 3 on a pair, 2, 3 and 4 on a three.

blocks.text:
# Fingers on the groups
Now give the groups their fingers. Every black key on the screen now has a finger number on it. Each card plays a pair or a three, lighting the keys as they sound; then it's your turn, starting from the lit key: tap them one after the other and **say each finger number out loud** as you tap. The first cards are for the right hand, on the higher keys: 2 and 3 on a pair, 2, 3 and 4 on a three. Then the left hand, on the lower keys: its fingers are numbered from the thumb too, so on a pair it's 3 and 2 going up, on a three 4, 3 and 2.

The screen is too small for three real fingers and can't see which finger you use, so here it's the numbers you're learning. At a table or a keyboard, rest those fingers on the groups and play them with the right fingers.

blocks.title: Fingers on the groups
blocks.about: Tap each lit key and say its finger number: right hand first, then left.

blocks.text:
# Playing a key, and letting it go
At a real keyboard, play a key with a **firm fingertip**: the tip keeps its shape and the key goes down. Then **let it go**: the key comes back up by itself and lifts your finger with it. You don't need to pull your finger up, and you don't need to press hard. Keep your wrist loose, as if it were floating. Loose doesn't mean sagging: the wrist stays about level with your forearm and knuckles, as in the sitting section.

On a phone or tablet screen there's no key to push down, so it's simply a light tap with your fingertip, then lifting off.

If you're at a keyboard now, try travelling on the groups the way pianists first learn to: put your right hand's fingers **2 and 3** on a group of two black keys in the middle, play them together, softly, and let your hand float up to the next group of two to the right. Keep going to the top. Then your left hand's **2 and 3**, travelling down to the left. Then the groups of three, with fingers **2, 3 and 4**.

# Copy what you see and hear
Now for listening. The app plays a short pattern on the black keys, and the keys light up as you hear them. Then you play it back, with any finger. It starts with one note, and each time you get it right the pattern grows by one. Once you've copied a pattern of three from memory, the game ends: that's the goal for today. **Hear it** is welcome whenever you want another listen; a pattern copied after it is good practice, but doesn't count toward the goal, so the game carries on.

Watch where the lit keys are within their group, the first key of a pair or the middle of three, and listen to whether the sound goes up or down.

blocks.title: Copy what you see and hear
blocks.about: The black keys around middle C: watch, listen, then play the pattern back.

blocks.text:
## If you'd like a challenge: by ear
This is optional, and harder. In the copying game, open **Level** and choose **5** (by ear): you'll hear the pattern, but the keys won't light up. The first note is always one of the same five black keys, so start by trying a key, listening, and moving higher or lower until it matches. If it feels like guesswork, that's fine: it gets easier with every lesson, and you can come back to it.

# Make up a tune
Here's something nice about the black keys: they fit together so well that almost anything you play on them sounds like music. Use any groups, high or low, fast or slow, and make up a little tune. If you're not sure how to start, play a few notes, play them again the same way, then change just the last note. There's no right or wrong here, and nothing is scored.

blocks.title: Make up a tune
blocks.about: Make up a tune on the black keys: any groups, high or low, fast or slow. Nothing is scored.

blocks.text:
# Check yourself
- Without looking at this page, tap a group of three black keys high up, then a group of two low down. Did you find them on the first try?
- Which fingers are 1 and 5? Wiggle them in each hand. Then 3, then 2.
- At a keyboard or table: make the C shape and drop the apples. Is your wrist loose?

# If this happens
- **You can't tell a group of two from a group of three.** Find a gap first: a place where two white keys sit together with no black key between them. Then count the black keys up to the next gap: two or three.
- **The key you want is off the edge of the screen.** Use the arrows beside the keys to move higher or lower.
- **At a keyboard, your fingers flatten out.** That's common at first. Make the C shape again, then play more gently: soft playing makes it easier to keep the fingertips firm.
- **Your shoulders or wrist feel tight.** Stop, let your arms hang, shake out your hands, and drop the apples.
- **You hear nothing.** Turn the volume up and check the device isn't on silent. In Settings, *Piano plays through* should say **Phone** (unless a MIDI keyboard is plugged in and you want its sound).
- **The copy game feels too quick.** The app waits for you; there's no clock. Listen and watch once more, then play.
